L125@P1: Figure: Cost of Different parts of Transformer Model
L126@P1: Due to the excessive cost of large-scale language
L127@P1: model pre-training, considerable efforts have been
L128@P1: made to train BERT progressively. BERT
L129@P1: transformers by design start from an inferior,
L130@P1: low-cost model and gradually grow the model to
L131@P1: increase the computational complexity. (Xiaotao Gu
L132@P1: et al.,2020)
L133@P1: So this model issue is systemic and by design. This is
L134@P1: profound when it comes to emotions recognition.
L135@P1: That brought us to analyze a paper which could
L136@P1: compare performance of sentiment (emotion)
L137@P1: recognition across multiple transformers.
L138@P1: 2.3 Transformers in Emotion Recognition: a
L139@P1: comparison of BERT, DistillBERT,
L140@P1: RoBERTa, XLNet and ELECTRA
L141@P1: In sentiment analysis, F1 scores for emotion
L142@P1: recognition, are pretty low across the spectrum.
L143@P1: According to Diogo Cortiz, et al 2021, ELECTRA
L144@P1: model, had the worst F1-score (.33), the other models
L145@P1: had more similar results. RoBERTa achieved the best
L146@P1: F1-score (.49), followed by DistillBERT (.48),
L147@P1-2: XLNet (.48), and then BERT (.46). ELECTRA doesnot rely on masked language such as BERT or
L148@P2: RoBERTa. Instead of masking the input and
L149@P2: predicting it, ELECTRA replaces tokens with
L150@P2: alternatives generated by a small generator network.
L151@P2: So for the diversity in transformer mix, I have
L152@P2: factored both BERT based transformers and
L153@P2: ELECTRA based transformers for our experiments.
L154@P2: I also want to understand biases & stereotypes to
L155@P2: mainly figure out if polarization has anything to do
L156@P2: with the unreliable nature of transformers. Follow up
L157@P2: with experiment to verify whether polarization does
L158@P2: occur even on a completely unbiased human labeled
L159@P2: ground truth. It would help showcase transformers’
L160@P2: role in sentiment polarization. First I want to
L161@P2: independently understand biases and de-biasing, any
L162@P2: ineffectiveness & lacunae in de-biasing.
L163@P2: 2.4 Usual Suspects : Biases, Stereotypes,
L164@P2: Dataset, Embeddings & De-biasing
L165@P2: Online texts, across genres, registers, domains, styles,
L166@P2: are riddled with human stereotypes” (Thomas
L167@P2: Manzini et al, 2019), is outlined in the paper “Black
L168@P2: is to Criminals, as Caucasian is to Police”. Paper
L169@P2: exclaims “in addition to possessing informative
L170@P2: features useful for a variety of NLP tasks, word
L171@P2: embeddings reflect and propagate social biases
L172@P2: present in training corpora (Caliskan et al., 2017;
L173@P2: Garg et al., 2018). Machine learning systems that use
L174@P2: embeddings can further amplify biases (Barocas and
L175@P2: Selbst, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017).”
L176@P2: De-biasing Solution
L177@P2: The multiclass de-biasing solutions offered (Thomas
L178@P2: Manzini et al, 2019) are hard & soft de-biasing. Hard
L179@P2: de-biasing, firstly required neutralize/equalize
L180@P2: not-gendered words, secondly, gendered words
L181@P2: embeddings are centered and their bias components
L182@P2: are equalized eg: male bias and female bias must be
L183@P2: equal magnitude. Soft De-biasing requires “learning a
L184@P2: projection of the embedding matrix that preserves the
L185@P2: inner product between bias and de-biased
L186@P2: embeddings while minimizing the projection onto the
L187@P2: bias subspace that should be neutral.”
L188@P2: Limitations
L189@P2: The de-biasing methods based on bias component
L190@P2: removal are insufficient to completely remove bias in
L191@P2: the embeddings, (Gonen and Goldberg, 2019), since
L192@P2: embeddings with similar biases are still clustered
L193@P2: together after bias component removal. However,
L194@P2: according to the author (Thomas Manzini et al),
L195@P2: increasing the size of the bias subspace reduces the
L196@P2: correlation of two variables and reduces the bias.
L197@P2: Source: [1904.04047]
L198@P2: The following paper added additional information
L199@P2: and relevant knowledge: Man is to Computer
L200@P2: Programmer as Woman is to Homemaker?
L201@P2: De-biasing Word Embeddings, Tolga Bolukbasi, et al,
L202@P2: Source: [1607.06520]. Other authors whose papers
L203@P2: provided insights in the related topic are Barocas &
L204@P2: Selbst, 2016; Zhao et al., 2017
L205@P2: During our experiments I did not observe significant,
L206@P2: consistent bias reduction across different datasets. As
L207@P2: I analyzed this issue further, I landed on this paper by
L208@P2: Po-Sen Huang, et al, 2020, which outlined that
L209@P2: de-biasing of word embeddings to be quite
L210@P2: ineffective. I needed a paper to validate and the
L211@P2: following did address that requirement.
L212@P2: 2.5 Evaluating sentiment bias in GPT-2
L213@P2: Po-Sen Huang, et al, 2020
L214@P2: In this paper, I found empirical sentiment distribution
L215@P2: of text generated by GPT-2. The paper reveals
L216@P2: systematic differences in sentiment depending on
L217@P2: occupation. To quantify sentiment bias, the author
L218@P2: proposes the use of individual and group fairness
L219@P2: metrics from the fair machine learning literature
L220@P2: (Dwork et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2019; Hardt et al.,
L221@P2: 2016). Rather than debiasing word embeddings, Lu et
L222@P2: al. (2018) proposed counterfactual data augmentation
L223@P2: as a remedy to occupation-specific gender biases. The
L224@P2: paper outlines the findings that it can be much
L225@P2: better to retain model performance than debiasing
L226@P2: word embeddings, especially in language modeling.
L227@P2: Source: [1911.03064]
L228@P2: Few of the related work are 1: Language Models are
L229@P2: Few-Shot Learners, Tom B. Brown, et al, 2020.
L230@P2: GPT-3 in spite of its superior performance still has
L231@P2: issues. GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to
L232@P2: training on large web corpora. Source: [2005.14165].
L233@P2: Related work 2: Bertscore: Evaluating text generation
L234@P2-3: with Bert. Tianyi Zhang, Varsha Kishore, Felix Wu,Kilian Q Weinberger, and Yoav Artzi. It is necessary
L235@P3: to both detect polarization and differentiate offensive
L236@P3: words from polite complaining texts, so as to treat
L237@P3: them accordingly.
L238@P3: 2.6 Offensive Language and Hate Speech
L239@P3: Detection
L240@P3: Understanding the relationship between polarity and
L241@P3: offensive languages is an input for the work.
L242@P3: “Differentiating if a text message belongs to hate
L243@P3: speech and offensive language is a key challenge in
L244@P3: automatic detection of toxic text content” (Bencheng
L245@P3: Wei, et al., 2021). In short, “Hate class usually has
L246@P3: more negative sentiment (Polarity) compared to
L247@P3: Neither and Of ensive.” Knowledge of Polarity helps
L248@P3: differentiate hate class from offensive and neither
L249@P3: class. So it is critical that a few more examples
L250@P3: perhaps are worth more than billions of parameters
L251@P3: (Yuval Kirstain, et al., 2021). Related work: Beyond
L252@P3: Accuracy: Behavioral Testing of NLP models with
L253@P3: Checklist (Marco et al 2020).
L254@P3: The polarization & loss of neutrality I observed both
L255@P3: in our applied AI projects and in research
L256@P3: experiments. There were a significant number of
L257@P3: papers on bias and stereotypes but not on sentiment
L258@P3: polarization or the loss of neutrality. This was indeed
L259@P3: a key motivator for us to take up the task of recording
L260@P3: our observations & writing a paper.
L261@P3: 3. Limitations
L262@P3: Key limitations are 1) Experiment Results Merge
L263@P3: Issues: The difficulty of merging of results coming
L264@P3: from different experiments on disparate sub systems
L265@P3: technology 2) Metric Issues: Non Translatability of
L266@P3: F1 Macro to the applied AI space covering business
L267@P3: rules. Lack of more Direct Correlation metrics for
L268@P3: Darkside impact because of business rules of
L269@P3: economical distribution of CSR Ticketing time &
L270@P3: CSR Bot resources, 3) Lack of Pipeline Neutrality,
L271@P3: Metric Transparency 4) Factual Inconsistencies 5)
L272@P3: Model Hallucination. 6) Subjectivity of Decisions in
L273@P3: Applied AI: the decision to act upon (Call to Action)
L274@P3: based on sentiment classification analysis is
L275@P3: multi-layered & subjective. Whether a customer
L276@P3: should be responded to, attended to, should a ticket
L277@P3: be raised is dependent on economics of time, budget
L278@P3: availability & workloads. In addition, there is the
L279@P3: emerging trend of Social Media Policing &
L280@P3: Conformance requirements resulting in loss of
L281@P3: shrinking the space for truthful sentiment expression,
L282@P3: loss of diversity of opinions and emergence of
L283@P3: monotonic predictably polarize-able sentiments.
L284@P3: Existing F1 Macro has limitations in measuring these
L285@P3: as it requires a multi-disciplinary metric approach.

L363@P4: 5. Metrics
L364@P4: The metrics that will form the basis for evaluation are
L365@P4: F1 Macro for standard baseline evaluation across
L366@P4: multiple transformers. I also used a more focused F1
L367@P4: Macro of Neutral Class for additional insights. Along
L368@P4: with neutral specific F1 Macro, I also use F1 Macro
L369@P4: for positive and negative sentiment class. This I
L370@P4: found was most appropriate given the scope was
L371@P4: focused on neutrality and sentiment polarization.
L372@P4: For future work, these are some of the metrics I
L373@P4: propose would be useful to measure loss of neutrality
L374@P4: at various stages inside the NLP pipeline.
L375@P4: - F1 Neutral_Precision
L376@P4: (Measure Pipeline Neutrality / Neutral_Precision)
L377@P4: - F1 Neutral_Loss_Type_1
L378@P4: - (Neutral_to_Negative Loss inside the Pipeline)
L379@P4: - F1 Neutral _Loss_Type_2
L380@P4: - (Neutral_to_Positive Loss inside the Pipeline)
L381@P4: Measuring and side by side reporting of neutral
L382@P4: mis-classification both with and without gold
L383@P4: reference across the NLP pipeline. This reporting
L384@P4: method will add tremendous transparency to the

L514@P6: 8. Analysis
L515@P6: In-spite of groundings & validation set having their
L516@P6: classes balanced, with equal polarity for positive,
L517@P6: negative and neutral, Transformer is still polarizing it
L518@P6: into negative labels with high score. From Table [5]
L519@P6: & Figure [1] there is a clear evidential proof for loss
L520@P6: of neutrality and polarization of sentiments. As I
L521@P6: increased the size of our training dataset, from Table
L522@P6: [8] & Figure [5] I did observe improvement in
L523@P6: Transformer F1 Macro Score. However the neutral
L524@P6: classification still suffered no matter what. I have
L525@P6: observed this trend with every increase in dataset
L526@P6: size. There is a progressive increase in F1 Score of
L527@P6: non-neutral class, and continued abysmal
L528@P6: performance of neutral class.
L529@P6: In a mix of ablation study and counter factual
L530@P6: analysis mode, when the same grounding dataset is
L531@P6: used but without the use of a transformer, the results
L532@P6: were incriminating. Even on the same sample size, a
L533@P6: lexicon based Vader did much better, and is able to
L534@P6: produce better F1 Score.
L535@P6: In processing sentiments on customer complaints
L536@P6: dataset, which has a negative tonality, the neural and
L537@P6: positive classes of Vader do suffer, but not as much as
L538@P6: Transformer based models. These NLP transformers
L539@P6: by default, start with the polarizing effect. Hence
L540@P6: expensive training is required to depolarize them,
L541@P6: with increasing training runs to hide the systemic
L542@P6: drawbacks without addressing it.
L543@P6: It is observed that neutrals belong to different vector
L544@P6: subspace(s) as compared to positives and negatives
L545@P6: and not on their margins. What the transformer is
L546@P6: doing is Gordian cutting of neutral and classifying
L547@P6: them as positive and negative. Result is the accuracy
L548@P6: improvement at the cost of wrongly classifying
L549@P6: neutral sentiments. DistilBert neutrality loss is still
L550@P6: very high compared to the ground truth and Vader
L551@P6: benchmark. Following cases further reveal other
L552@P6: issues accompanying NLP transformers

L555@P6: bright-side of transfer learning into the dark-side
